query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance and microscopic deformation of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate during sliding in the high-temperature operating regime are governed by the formation of a third body layer and the refinement of the microstructure, which are influenced by the presence of Cu and Ti in the alloy and the dynamic recrystallization mechanism.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: Addition of Cu and Ti to the alloy and application of friction stir processing (FSP) followed by annealing
generation.conditions: High-temperature operating regime, sliding velocity range of 0.5-3.5 m/s, and sliding distance range of 500-2000 m
generation.structural_mediator: Third body layer formation and microstructure refinement
generation.mechanism: Dynamic recrystallization mechanism and dislocation-induced deformation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance and reduced microscopic deformation
generation.baseline: Conventional metal substrate without high-entropy alloy coating
generation.boundary: High-temperature operating regime, specific sliding velocity and distance ranges
generation.uncertainty: Influence of other factors such as load, surface roughness, and environmental conditions on the wear resistance and microscopic deformation

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear test with varying sliding velocity and distance, and microstructural characterization using SEM and EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SWR and COF do not decrease with the addition of Cu and Ti to the alloy and application of FSP followed by annealing, and if the microstructure refinement is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

FSP refines the surface through the heat evolved from friction with no additional heat input or release of toxic fumes in the process,. This attribute of FSP made it considered to be a green process and green fabrication technique. The heat generated in the FSP also greatly influence the strength and properties. Pan et al. carried out FSP on stainless steel and obtained grain refinement at a sub-micron level with a maximum microhardness of 779HV. The refinement of grains and the dissolution of particles improved the corrosion resistance of the material as well. Xie et al. carried out FSP on duplex stainless steel and observed ultra refinement in grains due to dynamic recrystallisation with a large amount of high angle grain boundary. The yield strength of the processed steel was comparable with the base metal due to the formation of microvoids. Further exploring, FSP followed by a heat treatment process has resulted in homogeneous and defect-free microstructure aiding in the improvement of properties. Studies have reported an improvement in tribological properties after FSP of steels that support the utilisation of the technique in the mentioned applications. Tinubu et al. processed stainless steel by FSP and observed refined grains with an average size of 2–3 µm which subsequently improved microhardness by 34%. The improved microhardness contributed to better wear performance through microabrasion in the sample. Aldajah et al. equipped FSP on high carbon steel to improve wear strength by modifying the surface. The wear rate was significantly decreased after the FSP on dry conditions and even more decreased under lubrication.
